t: An unknown author, named Vishnusharma in the prelude, set animal fables inside a frame story to teach three princes nīti, the wise conduct of life.
Its Middle Persian version of about 550 CE is lost, but the Arabic Kalīla wa Dimna made from it in about 750 became the source of most European versions.
Scholars disagree whether it favours unscrupulous Machiavellian politics or demands ethical conduct from those in high office.
dyk: A woman leaves her child with a pet mongoose, finds blood on its mouth and kills it, then finds the child alive and the mongoose's blood to be a snake's. The story is told in the fifth book, whose characters are almost all human.
ev: Scholarly consensus places the composition of the Panchatantra around this year, which Patrick Olivelle calls only an educated guess
The physician Borzuy translates the work from Sanskrit into Pahlavi, the Middle Persian language
Ibn al-Muqaffa translates the work into Arabic as Kalīla wa Dimna
Rabbi Joel makes a Hebrew version, the source of most European versions
John of Capua's Latin Directorium Humanae Vitae is printed
Sir Thomas North publishes the first English translation, The Morall Philosophie of Doni
Franklin Edgerton publishes his reconstruction of the original Sanskrit text
Patrick Olivelle's translation, based on Edgerton's reconstruction, is published by Oxford University Press

f.made: An unknown author, named Vishnusharma in some recensions and Vasubhaga in others, both possibly fictitious pen names; probably a Hindu, drawing on older oral and literary traditions
f.form: Five treatises of fables in Sanskrit verse and prose inside a frame story, with a short introduction; embedded tales and epigrammatic verses; Book 1 is about 45% of the length
f.where: No Sanskrit text before 1000 CE survives; it is read in Sanskrit recensions, in Indian and Southeast Asian versions and in translations into over 50 languages
f.known: Animal fables with human virtues and vices; the jackals Damanaka and Karataka; the mongoose and the woman; nīti, the wise conduct of life; Kalila wa Dimna; the Fables of Bidpai; the Hebrew, Latin and English versions
